extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, students/scholars of drama and literature, literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for composing and evaluating tragic drama (plot, character, diction, chorus, and stagecraft) based on Aristotle's Poetics and commentary. Covers principles of character-consistency, plot construction (tying/loosing), probability, disclosure devices, diction/prosody, and the role of the chorus and spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters should be good
rubrics_metrics.description: That the characters should be good: we require in the drama persons with whom we sympathize, and where such are wanting the dramatist will scarcely be able either to arouse or gratify our interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good characters arouse sympathy; Aristotle argues against the presence of a pure villain (compound transition) because villains tend toward the comic. Examples and commentary: dramatists must present persons who elicit sympathy to sustain interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speech or conduct must be psychological
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech or Conduct will be psychological, if it reveal any intention with which [a course is adopted or rejected], and the character delineated will be good if the intention be so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions and speech must reveal the agent's intentions; moral quality of character depends on intentions. Commentary notes social/status relativity (e.g., women and slaves have different virtuous norms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of traits
rubrics_metrics.description: It should be appropriate; for it is possible for the person to be of brave character, yet for the species of courage to be unsuitable, if the person be a woman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traits must suit the person's species/status/role. The text debates translators' misreadings and stresses suitability relative to social role and dramatic plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Likeness (fidelity to historical character)
rubrics_metrics.description: It should be like; i.e. the historical character portrayed must not be seriously altered in the reproduction. Achilles must not be made cowardly or Odysseus brainless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical figures should retain essential traits; limited departures permitted to heighten aesthetic emotion depending on audience and celebrity of the character (e.g., Schiller and Don Carlos).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equability (consistency of character)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fourth point is equability; even if the character portrayed be fitful, and such a character be the theme, it ought to be uniformly fitful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters must act consistently within their established temperament; avoid sudden incompatible changes (example: Iphigeneia differing in scenes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid immoral psychology (no needless knavery)
rubrics_metrics.description: An example of immoral psychology is any unnecessary [case of knavery] ... A poet can only be charged with immorality when he introduces a knave without anything making such introduction necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not make characters wicked without justifying reasons within the plot or class-contrast needs; knavery may be acceptable if inherent to class/role or makes the play effective (e.g., Aegisthus in Agamemnon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incidents should follow laws of nature and moral certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: In the character, as in the grouping of the incidents, you should always study laws of nature and moral certainty, so that it should become either necessary or morally certain for the kind of character to say or do the kind of thing, and in the particular order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot incidents must arise plausibly from human nature and moral probability so actions feel necessary or at least likely; this underpins believability and emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Events must evolve from characters (avoid deus ex machina)
rubrics_metrics.description: The evolution of the story should come about from the characters themselves, and not by a deus ex machina ... the deus ex machina may, however, be employed for events in the background of the drama ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreground resolutions must be motivated by character and plot; supernatural or machine-like contrivances are permissible only for background or to reveal matters beyond human knowledge. Example: Aegeus in Medea is criticized as an unnecessary deus ex machina.

rubrics_metrics.name: No unaccountable action in the foreground
rubrics_metrics.description: In the proceedings themselves there should be nothing unaccountable; if there is, it should be in the background of the play, as in the Oedipus of Sophocles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid shocking or inexplicable stage events that break audience belief (e.g., resurrection from a temple). Such elements, if used, should be carefully motivated or relegated to background exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray characters like portrait-painters (improve upon likeness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy ... should imitate good portrait-painters; for they too, while reproducing the peculiar features, without impairing the likeness, improve upon it; so the poet ... should represent people who are irascible, slothful or with similar failings in their characters, should represent them as such, yet virtuous withal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capture distinctive features faithfully but heightened to produce nobility or aesthetic effect (Homer's Achilles is an example: hard but heroic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful of impressions indirectly connected with art
rubrics_metrics.description: While observing these rules, he should also be careful of the impressions only indirectly connected with his own art; for here, too, mistakes can often be made ... a tragedy must have psychology ... it need not trench on religion or politics, but, if it does so, the prejudices of the audience should not be hurt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider audience sensibilities: avoid needlessly offending religious or political sentiments that can wreck reception; understand changing beliefs across generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of mistaken identity: prefer scientific (natural) tokens
rubrics_metrics.description: The best Disclosure of Mistaken Identity is that which proceeds without violation of probability from the actual composition of the story ... Only this sort can dispense with fictitious evidence of identity and 'necklaces.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer identity revelations that arise naturally from the plot (e.g., Oedipus, Iphigeneia). Tokens (congenital scars, inherited marks, preserved objects) vary in scientificity: inherited/typical signs are more 'scientific' (general) than purely individual tokens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of disclosure and their ranking
rubrics_metrics.description: Tokens ... The second sort are proofs of identity fabricated by the poet ... The third process is effected by a mention or a sight which agitates the hero ... The fourth process starts from observation of coincidence ... The best Disclosure ... is that which proceeds without violation of probability ... The next best are those which are due to the observation of coincidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rank disclosures: (1) natural, probabilistic disclosures arising from story composition; (2) observation-of-coincidence devices; (3) emotionally-triggered recognition; (4) poet-fabricated proofs; fabricated proofs are least scientific and less satisfying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use misleading of the audience carefully (disappointed expectation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Misleading of the audience: if you would introduce a surprise, it should only be in the form of a disappointed expectation. The spectator had made up his mind that something definite was going to happen, and suddenly it all changes ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surprise should be structured as a subversion of an established expectation; obvious clues can be used to mislead but must still respect narrative probability and avoid arbitrary deception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualize the story while composing
rubrics_metrics.description: While composing the story ... you should, so far as possible, visualize it; the poet will thus be, as it were, an eyewitness of the events, most likely to discover what is appropriate and alive to inconsistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceptualize scenes as living pictures/pantomime rather than merely linguistic constructs; stage action must be intelligible in visual terms—'the dramatist must be a sculptor, perhaps even a painter, but on no account a talker.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Assist composition by gestures and simulated emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: You should also, while composing, assist the work by your gestures so far as possible; for a fictitious emotion emanating from a reality of the same kind is most realistic; he who is feeling distress or anger can also counterfeit it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors/actors may use physical gesture and simulated emotion (autosuggestion) to achieve realism. Commentary notes debate: some authorities insist emotion must be cooled for craft; others endorse autosuggestion and prepared physical expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: State the argument first, then compose scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the argument has already been treated or whether you are treating it yourself for the first time, should be first stated in the abstract, then filled in with scenes to the requisite length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline the central argument/plot principle and the principles you wish to illustrate before composing. Use names and scenes germane to the argument; differentiate between concise tragic scenes and spun-out romantic interludes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity and unity: tragedy must not become a romance
rubrics_metrics.description: It cannot be too often repeated that a Tragedy must not be turned into a Romance, i.e. a piece with endless interludes ... In a Tragedy—you never know what will happen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain concision and unity of action; avoid sprawling episodic treatment (e.g., dramatizing the whole Iliad at length) — tragedies should focus on tying/loosing structure rather than episodic interludes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tying and loosing (structural division)
rubrics_metrics.description: In every Tragedy one part is the tying, the other the loosing. The tying is ... from the commencement to the exact point at which the change of fortune commences ... a real loosing is one that occupies the space from the transition-point to the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design plot so the 'tying' (setup/complication) leads inevitably to a 'loosing' (resolution) around a clear transition point; both must be mastered to secure tragic effect (examples: Lynceus of Theodectes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Four varieties of tragedy and combining elements
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four varieties: the Plot Tragedy (interest turns on Irony of Fate and Disclosure of Mistaken Identity); the Emotional Tragedy; the Psychological Tragedy; the Tragedy of appropriate expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to combine elements of plot-structure, emotional intensity, psychological depth, and apt expression; if impossible, include as many effective elements as feasible. Identity of tragedies depends on story (tying/loosing) more than characters alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Chorus should participate as an actor
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus should regard itself as one of the actors and a member of the entirety, and should participate in the performance ... With most authors the Choric songs have no more to do with the story of one Tragedy than of another ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chorus should be integrated into action (as in Sophocles), help start and spread emotion among the audience, and avoid being a detachable element (do not casually transfer songs between plays).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction / Intelligence: speech as instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: Every factor has now been discussed except Diction or Intelligence. To the province of Intelligence belong all the operations of which Speech is the instrument, of which the divisions are demonstration and refutation, the arousing of emotions, such as pity, fear, anger, etc., exaggeration and depreciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use diction to perform logical demonstration/refutation and to elicit emotions; style must shape the material to produce the desired pathetic, grand, or plausible effects. Rhetorical patterns appropriate to situations should be applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study of elocution, prosody, and parts of speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the studies grouped round Language one is the Classification of Sentences ... Of Speech in general the following are the parts: Letter, Combination, Conjunction (Separative), Noun, Verb, Inflexion, Statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand technical elements of language for dramatic effect: prosody (vowels, semi-vowels, mutes), combinations, conjunctions/separatives, nouns/verbs/inflections, sentence-classes (command, prayer, narrative, menace, question, reply). Knowledge belongs to elocution but affects poetic diction and delivery.
